title: The Testimony Problem
body:
Courts have long treated eyewitness testimony as among the strongest evidence available. A witness who saw the event and describes it under oath carries a weight that circumstantial evidence rarely matches, and juries respond accordingly. Confidence expressed on the stand is read as a proxy for accuracy.

Experimental psychology has steadily undermined that assumption. In controlled studies, participants shown a staged incident and questioned afterwards produce accounts that drift in predictable directions. Details absent from the original scene appear in later retellings. Faces are reassigned. The drift is not random: it moves toward whatever the questioner's phrasing implies. Asked how fast cars were going when they smashed into each other, participants report higher speeds than those asked about cars that contacted each other, and are more likely to recall broken glass that was never there.

What makes this difficult for courts is that the witnesses in these studies are not lying and do not know they are wrong. Their confidence often rises as their accuracy falls, because each retelling rehearses the account and rehearsal feels like corroboration. A witness who has repeated a description twenty times before trial will deliver it more fluently than one recalling it fresh, and fluency reads as certainty to everyone in the room.

Several jurisdictions now require judges to instruct juries that confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. Whether such instructions work is contested; some studies find they make jurors sceptical of all testimony rather than calibrated about any of it. The narrower reforms have fared better. Recording the witness's confidence at the moment of the first identification, before any feedback, preserves a measurement that later proceedings cannot inflate. It does not solve the problem, but it stops the record from being quietly overwritten.

title: Who Owns a Translation
body:
A translator working from a fifteenth-century manuscript faces a choice that has no neutral answer. Rendering the text word for word produces something faithful to the original syntax and largely unreadable. Rendering it into fluent modern prose produces something readable that has quietly acquired a voice the original never had.

The scholarly convention through most of the twentieth century favoured the first approach. Fidelity meant staying close to the source, and a translation that read awkwardly was taken as evidence of restraint. Notes at the foot of the page carried whatever the surface could not.

That convention has weakened. Critics observed that word-for-word rendering is not actually neutral: it imports the grammatical habits of the source language into the target, producing an effect of strangeness that the original readers would not have felt. A medieval reader did not experience the text as archaic. Preserving the archaism therefore introduces a distance that was not present, which is itself a distortion, merely one that looks like caution.

The alternative carries its own cost, and translators who take it say so plainly. Fluency requires choosing among possible meanings where the original was ambiguous, and every such choice removes an option the reader might otherwise have weighed. A footnote can flag the most consequential of these, but not all of them; a text with a note on every line is no longer a translation but an apparatus.

What has changed is less the practice than the disclosure. Contemporary translations increasingly carry prefaces setting out what the translator decided and why. The decisions are no more avoidable than before, but they are now visible, which lets a reader judge the translation as an argument rather than receiving it as a transparent window.
